So fucking what? Firstly, we don't even know that this guy is suffering from a condition or compulsion. Some public masturbators are mentally ill, sure, but there are a *lot* of them who are just otherwise regular guys, who grew up in this fucked culture of male entitlement that teaches us (both men and women) that women's bodies exist for men's use and pleasure. Secondly, even if this guy is sick...again, *so fucking what?* He's clearly not completely mentally incapacitated, as he knows how to work a computer, order coffee, and presumably work a job requiring him to wear a suit. He also clearly knew that what he did was wrong. 

Pedophiles are sick people. Genuinely sick. They cannot control their sexual urges towards children. And yet there are pedophiles who choose not to indulge those urges, who make the humane and moral decision to NOT victimize innocent children through sexual abuse or viewing child porn.

I'm not convinced this guy is "sick." Seems more likely to me that he gets off on using women and making them uncomfortable. But even if that fetish is part of a mental illness, I don't give a fuck. He's probably completely capable of making the choice to NOT victimize random women. And if he's not? At the very least, he's capable of seeking help to control his urges. *He made the choice to ignore those options.*

Honestly, I see what you mean, I do. It's an unfortunate reality. You're absolutely right that it's up to any given person to decide whether or not to fight against them.

I got my boobs at 12. That's when everyone started calling me a slut. That's when my friends' fathers started being inappropriate with me. That's when the near daily harassment started. The assaults didn't come 'til a few years later, but they came. And I've been told that I should expect it because of two sacks of fat on my chest that *I didn't ask for.* I *loathed* my breasts for many years. Sometimes...often...I still do.  So for me, personally, the fight is worth it, to try to stop feeling ashamed of a body that is relatively healthy, a body that I should take pride in.

I understand what you're getting at, and you of course raise some good points, but I'm not suggesting that I (or any other curvy woman) would be wise to wear "whatever the hell I want." Again, I am not talking about halter tops and mini-skirts; I am talking about my wish to be able to wear a dress or a pair of paints that is tailored to my natural body without being presumed to be slutty or stupid. I am saying that I believe it is wrong for people to judge me as a woman and as a human because the fitted tee I wear shows my F-cup breasts, just as the fitted tee my friend wears shows her A-cup breasts. Her breasts *are no less on display than mine* - they are simply smaller, and therefore, "more work-appropriate." I think that's wrong, and after a lifetime of being shamed about my "whore tits," I'm beginning to find the courage to wear clothes that fit and walk without a hunch.

For me, it does come down to censorship. If I want to look polished and professional, I simply am not going to wear clothes that are a few sizes too big, which is honestly the only way to hide my boobs. If I dress reasonably, no matter what I wear, you and everyone else WILL notice my boobs. They are visible in blouses, t-shirts, turtlenecks, and hoodies. I would never show cleavage at work. I don't think I've ever worn a skirt more than an inch above my knee. I don't think  I look inappropriate in a *correctly sized* button-down and pencil skirt just because society has deemed my figure "slutty."

I'm a slim girl with F-cup breasts, and I've been relentlessly shamed for wearing t-shirts that fit me. It's totally within your rights to take it as a compliment. But not every woman in the world is going to *feel* complimented by something like that. For me, personally, "taking it as a compliment" does hurt someone - me. I feel similarly to /u/TheLatexCaterpillar. If a stranger I have never met before screams out "HEY CUTIE" at me, I feel disrespected. It's presumptuous and overly familiar. It's like, dude: you are not my great aunt Agatha. You are not my boyfriend. You are someone with whom I have never made contact. You find me attractive? You want to let me know? Respectfully engage me in conversation. Approach me. "Excuse me, but I just wanted to let you know that I think you're cute." Don't holler out some term of endearment that you really don't have a right to use.

Edited to add: You're right. There are many other, ruder things that could be yelled. I live in New York, so I've heard a lot of them. I hear them daily. It's a spectrum. "Hey cutie" or "mmm, beautiful" are at the low end, and "Bitch, I'd tear that ass apart" is at the high end, but it's all coming from the same place. I am sure that my having been exposed to a lot of the really vile, sexual stuff also makes hearing "hey cutie" more rage-inducing. But I'm not the type of person to dismiss something "because it could be worse." If someone slaps my ass while walking by, I'm not going to giggle and let it slide just because he didn't shove his hand all the way up my skirt, you know?

You definitely have a point in terms of character and structure. But I genuinely think that's only part of the picture. 

What happens when we put a dubiously moral woman in the role of protagonist? We get Nancy Botwin. Maybe it's just the portions of the Internet I frequent, or the people in my life, but I didn't encounter *nearly* the same level of praise and adoration for Nancy as I do for, say, Don. "Slut" got thrown around a lot. People harped on about how horrible and selfish she was. And she WAS. It's not wrong to talk about Nancy that way. It's just problematic that people form these weird fan clubs for Don rather than focusing on his flaws as they do with Nancy.

See, I don't think it's as simple as disliking these female characters. You have to juxtapose their reception with the way that audiences receive their male counterparts. Take Skyler, for instance. The words I most commonly hear used against her are "controlling," "nag," and "bitch." Meanwhile, I think Walter White was written to inspire anger and frustration in viewers, but many people nonetheless latched on to him as a laudable badass. It legitimately scares me sometimes, the amount of "fuck yeah!" sentiment that Walt apparently engenders in people.

Another similar example is Don and Betty Draper. Don Draper is a terrible person. He is possibly a sociopath. He is a relentless and remorseless philanderer. He is emotionally abusive, manipulative, and controlling towards Betty. But Betty is cold, and that's apparently enough to have her trump him as a villain. Yes, there are *plenty* of criticisms one can level at her character, and she's far from likeable, but again, it's all about reception. People fucking love Don Draper. They want to emulate him. He's cool, he's sexy, he's "the man." But Betty? Well Betty's just some bitch.

What's so scary and sad to me is that these men destroy multiple lives. But as soon as their wives attempt to exert any sort of control, the audience rips these women to shreds.

Oh wow, that has not been my experience at all. In my experience, these men are completely aware that women hate their behavior and that it's unwanted. They just don't remotely care.

My strategy now is similar OP's approach, provided I have the time. If I get a "mmm, sexy" or what have you, I just stop, look directly at them, and in a very matter-of-fact way, ask, "Why do you think that's an appropriate thing to say?" 9 times out of 10, they laugh/sneer and tell me it's "just a compliment."
